title: Re-run the customer provisioning journey unattended after self-setup
description:
**Phase 1 of 5.**

- **Blocked by:** nothing — all three self-setup stories are closed
- **Blocks, in practice:** publishing the self-setup offer on `chatticus-b4f849`

---

## Why this exists

`chatticus-9c8dbf`, `chatticus-070cb4` and `chatticus-7622fd` are all closed. Each met its own DoD and each was live-accepted individually.

**Three green cards is not the same claim as "the journey works unattended."** `chatticus-b88c0a` measured six person-steps, four of which needed an operator at a CLI. Those four each have a card that is now closed. Nobody has re-run the journey to confirm the path composes.

The original objection to publishing `chatticus-b4f849` was that the page promises something the product cannot do. That objection is only retired by a run, not by a card count.

## What to run

The `chatticus-b88c0a` journey again, as a customer, **with no operator kernel calls at all.** The discipline that made the first run trustworthy applies unchanged: placeholders in the wiki, real ids in gitignored `AGENTS.local.md`, every deviation labeled, stop and record at the first failure rather than pushing through.

Any operator step that turns out to still be required is a finding, not a workaround. Record it and stop — a labeled stop is a result.

## What to measure

- **Person-steps, again.** The number to compare against is four-of-six. If it is now zero-of-N, the self-setup offer is honest. If it is not, that is exactly what `chatticus-b4f849` needs to know before the page ships.
- **Elapsed wall-clock**, kept separate from the ~19 min provisioning figure, which excluded consumer AWS signup and everything after.
- **Every place the instructions were wrong.** Same as last time: the most valuable output and the easiest to skip while heads-down making it work.

## Also worth confirming on this run

The image staleness seen during file-recycle acceptance (`HOST_IMAGE_STALE_CHROMIUM_EXECUTOR_ONLY`, fixed by an operator repush) was correctly judged not a product bug. But an operator repush is a **person-step per customer account**, and image updates recur. If it appears again in an unattended run, it belongs in the person-step count and in the invitation-rate math.

## Done when

The runbook has a second timed entry with a person-step count taken under no-operator conditions, and `chatticus-b4f849` can cite it — or the run stops at a labeled failure and that failure has a card.

The repeated Google prompt after an already-completed sign-in is a product defect, not only a cookie-jar split. comments.author: home
comments.text:
## Sequencing: fix `chatticus-5e4c9a` before running this (2026-09-08)

This card measures person-steps under no-operator conditions, and the number to beat is four-of-six from `chatticus-b88c0a`.

**A known auth defect is live right now that will contaminate that number.** `chatticus-5e4c9a`: reloading `dev.chattic.us` while signed in shows the sign-in page again. It already caused real confusion during testing about whether a login had happened at all.

The customer journey almost certainly involves reloads — after CloudFormation returns, after enablement, while waiting on a deploy. Each one currently looks like a sign-out. That leaves two bad options:

- **Count it** as a person-step, and publish a number that is wrong the moment `5e4c9a` lands.
- **Don't count it**, and the run is no longer measuring what a customer experiences.

Either way the run has to be repeated. Better to fix first and measure once.

## Suggested order

1. **`chatticus-5e4c9a`** — the reload bug. Two definite config faults are already identified on that card (no `offline_access`, so no refresh token; `prompt: select_account` set globally, which also blocks iframe silent renew).
2. **`chatticus-98f4f6`** — batch it with the above. Both edit `buildUserManagerSettings` in `web/lib/auth.ts`. Deciding where the session token lives and fixing scope/prompt is **one edit and one review**, not two.
3. **This card**, on a clean build.

## Not a reason to stall

If the auth fix turns out to be slow, run this anyway and **record the reload behaviour explicitly as a known defect** rather than as a customer person-step. What must not happen is the number being published without saying which it was.
